record.original_question: Given a digraph D, can its arc set always be partitioned into two linear forests, where a linear forest means a disjoint union of directed paths?

evidence.quote: A linear forest is the union of directed paths.
Algorithmic question : can we partition the arcs of a diraph D into two linear forests ?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A digraph $D=(V,A)$ is a finite directed graph (loops and multiple arcs are excluded). A directed path is a sequence of distinct vertices $v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k$ together with the arcs $v_0v_1,v_1v_2,\dots,v_{k-1}v_k$. A linear forest in $D$ is a subdigraph whose arc set is a disjoint union of (the arc sets of) directed paths; equivalently, a spanning subdigraph in which every vertex has in-degree at most $1$ and out-degree at most $1$, and whose underlying graph is acyclic.

A partition of the arc set $A$ into two linear forests is a decomposition $A=A_1\sqcup A_2$ such that, for each $i\in\{1,2\}$, the spanning subdigraph $(V,A_i)$ is a linear forest.

Necessarily, in any such decomposition every vertex of $D$ must have in-degree at most $2$ and out-degree at most $2$. The problem is the following:

Is it true that every digraph $D$ with maximum in-degree at most $2$ and maximum out-degree at most $2$ admits a partition of its arc set into two linear forests? Equivalently, design an algorithm that, given such a digraph $D$, decides whether $A(D)$ can be partitioned into two linear forests, and produces such a partition when one exists.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is connected to the linear arboricity of digraphs introduced by Nakayama and Péroche (1987), whose conjecture (every $d$-regular digraph has linear arboricity $d+1$) was disproved in 2017 for symmetric complete digraphs by He et al. A 2024 dichotomy result by Aubian, Hörsch et al. shows that decomposing a digraph into a $k$-bounded and an $\ell$-bounded directed linear forest is polynomial when $k+\ell\le 3$ and NP-complete otherwise, indicating that the unrestricted version of decomposition into two linear forests is computationally hard. The general existence question for digraphs of maximum in- and out-degree two is still not fully settled.

status_evidence.title: Complexity results on the decomposition of a digraph into directed linear forests and out-stars
status_evidence.snippet: Full dichotomy: decomposing a digraph into a k-bounded and an ℓ-bounded directed linear forest is polynomial if k+ℓ≤3 and NP-complete otherwise.
status_evidence.claim: The decomposition problem into two linear forests is computationally hard in general, with a sharp dichotomy.

status_evidence.title: Linear arboricity of digraphs - Nakayama, Péroche
status_evidence.snippet: Introduces linear arboricity of digraphs and conjectures bounds for d-regular digraphs.
status_evidence.claim: Foundational conjecture on linear arboricity of digraphs; later shown false for symmetric complete digraphs.

status_evidence.title: The List Linear Arboricity of Digraphs
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work continues to study linear arboricity bounds for digraphs.
status_evidence.claim: The area remains active with partial results.
